title: Break It 'Til You Make It: Building the Self-Improving Stack for AI Agents - Aparna Dhinakaran

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central focus is a multi-layered agent evaluation framework spanning tool call, trajectory, and session levels, plus dual self-improvement loops for eval prompts. The evaluation methodology is cross-domain and demonstrated on Arize's developer co-pilot product. The talk covers offline evaluation design, production tracing for bottleneck identification, and iterative improvement of both agents and evals. Requires familiarity with AI agents, tool calling, and prompt engineering per stated prerequisites. Conference presentation with slides and a live product demo. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting excerpts.

summary: Aparna Dhinakaran, co-founder of Arize, addresses the difficulty of building and evaluating AI agents beyond the prototype stage. She observes that teams commonly iterate on prompts and models in Excel sheets, relying on subjective judgment across a few examples before deploying—a practice that makes it hard to systematically track improvements or involve non-technical stakeholders like product managers and domain experts in the evaluation process. After deployment, identifying bottlenecks—whether a specific sub-agent or tool call consistently produces poor responses—remains challenging. She introduces a layered evaluation framework. First, tool call evaluation checks whether the agent selects the correct tool and passes the correct arguments given conversation context. Second, trajectory evaluation examines whether the agent calls tools in the right order across an entire trace, since incorrect ordering wastes tokens and degrades outputs. Third, session-level evaluation addresses multi-turn conversations, asking whether the agent maintains context from prior turns, stays consistent in tone, and avoids repetitive questioning. Using Arize's own co-pilot as a live demo, she shows an orchestration-worker architecture with a planner routing to multiple tools. A high-level view across all agent paths reveals search-related queries fail roughly half the time—a clear bottleneck. Drilling into individual traces shows tool selection is correct but argument passing is wrong, pinpointing the fix. She then presents the talk's central thesis: self-improvement requires two iterative loops running simultaneously. One loop improves the agent application prompts by identifying failures, annotating, and refining outputs. The other loop improves the eval prompts themselves, since evals can miscorrectly label outputs as wrong—building up a golden data set and consistently refining it ensures evals stay reliable. Both loops go hand in hand to create a strong product experience. She closes by pointing to Arize Phoenix, an open-source product for learning and testing these techniques, and Arize for running evaluations at scale on production data.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Aparna introduces herself as co-founder of Arize, which builds development tools for agent evaluation, observability, and tracing. She explains that building agents is hard due to extensive iteration at the prompt, model, and tool call levels. Teams commonly work in Excel sheets, swapping prompts with subjective judgments on a few examples before going live. Systematic tracking of improvements and inclusion of non-technical stakeholders are persistent challenges, both pre- and post-deployment.

sections.title: Evaluation Framework Overview
sections.summary: She outlines the talk structure: evaluating at the tool call level, then trajectory-level (order of tool calls across a trace), then multi-turn session evaluation (context retention across turns). She previews a self-improvement approach where both the agent and the evals themselves must improve, and mentions a live demo will follow slides.

sections.title: Tool Call Evaluation and Arize Demo
sections.summary: Using Arize's own co-pilot as a dogfooded example, she shows an orchestration-worker architecture with a planner routing to multiple tools. A high-level view across all agent paths reveals search Q&A failing roughly half the time. Drilling into traces shows eval results at trace level and tool call level—the tool call selection is correct but argument passing is incorrect, pinpointing the specific fix needed.

sections.title: Trajectory Evaluation
sections.summary: She explains that agents often make many tool calls in sequence, not just one. Trajectory evaluation checks whether the agent calls tools in the correct order across a series of steps, consistently converging on a fixed number of steps or veering off into different orderings that waste tokens and produce wrong outputs.

sections.title: Multi-Turn Session Evaluation
sections.summary: She addresses multi-turn conversations where humans and agents exchange multiple messages. Key evaluation questions include whether the agent is consistent in tone, whether it repeats questions unnecessarily, and whether it retains context from previous turns (n minus 1) to answer the nth turn well. She recommends session-level evaluations as a core part of agent evaluation, showing an example from another project.

sections.title: Dual Self-Improvement Loops and Closing
sections.summary: She explains that evaluating the agent application prompt to identify failures, annotate, and refine outputs is something many teams already do. The critical insight is that eval prompts—the crux of identifying failure cases—must not remain static. Teams should consistently check eval outcomes because evals can miscorrectly label outputs as wrong, and iterate on eval prompts just as they do on application prompts, building up a golden data set. This creates two parallel iterative loops: one for agent application prompts and one for eval prompts, both going hand in hand for a strong product experience. She closes by pointing to Arize Phoenix (open-source) for hands-on learning and Arize for running evaluations on production data.
